rationale: Documenting the mechanism the account had been treating implicitly: the application side ordering duties are enforced by fatal guards rather than clamped, which tells a reviewer exactly which client misbehaviour the module refuses to absorb and why the before/after observations of this run are the right shape. This is a client-contract behaviour, not a defect: the guards fire on the application's own reports, so a misbehaving application can only bring down its own node.

investigations.question: How does the module enforce the ordering and completion duties it places on the application, and can an application's own misreporting advance or rewind the applied/committed bookkeeping instead of being rejected?
investigations.hypothesis: The duties are enforced by fatal guards: rewriting entries at or below the commit index, committing past the last index, reporting a committed index below the applied one or above the committed one, and accepting application for an index past committed are each a panic, so misreporting cannot quietly corrupt the bookkeeping; the only tolerated adjustments are saturating counters and pausing further application until progress is acknowledged.
investigations.discriminator: Source: whether each of the four ordering violations reaches a guard that panics rather than a clamp or an ignored write, and whether the resume path for the one tolerated condition (paused application) is the application's own acknowledgement rather than an unbounded wait.

knowledge.statement: The application-facing ordering duties are enforced by fatal guards, not by clamping: appending entries whose predecessor is below the commit index panics, committing to an index past the last index panics, reporting an applied index outside [previously applied, committed] panics, accepting application for an index past committed panics, and computing a non-positive application size budget panics. The only tolerated adjustments are non-fatal: applied-to bookkeeping clamps its outstanding-size counter at zero, and application is paused (applyingEntsPaused) once the outstanding size reaches the configured limit, resuming when the application's acknowledgement, via Applied or the storage apply response, brings the outstanding size down. Entry rewriting above the commit index is allowed by design, which is how a follower replaces a divergent uncommitted tail.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot, source reading only (no execution claimed): log.go 136-140 (append guard), 322-328 (commitTo guard), 330-341 (appliedTo guard and counter clamp), 344-356 (acceptApplying guard and the pause condition), 234-238 (budget guard), with the client duties stated in node.go around ReadIndex/Ready and in the Ready struct documentation. The guards fire on values the module itself passes (from Ready/Advance) as well as on values an application reports in MsgStorageApplyResp, so a misreporting application is the party that trips them.

interpretations.rationale: The question is answered from the sources and the answer is a design fact rather than a defect. Each ordering violation an application could commit - rewriting committed entries, committing past the last index, applying out of order or past committed, or accepting application past committed - reaches a guard that panics, so the bookkeeping cannot be quietly advanced or rewound by a misreporting client; the two tolerated cases are treated differently on purpose (the outstanding-size counter saturates at zero, and further application pauses until the client acknowledges progress). Two consequences matter for reading this run's evidence: first, the module's before/after style observations are meaningful because the counters it reports cannot have been silently clamped into place; second, a client that misreports brings down its own process rather than corrupting the state machine, so the guards protect the module and the peer set without pretending to validate the application. Rewriting entries above the commit index is deliberately not a violation, which is exactly how a follower truncates a divergent uncommitted tail.
counterevidence: One guard can also fire on values the module computes itself (the application size budget), which would indicate an internal inconsistency rather than client misbehaviour; the account therefore does not claim every panic implies a faulty client.
limitations: Source reading only: no execution triggered a guard in this run, so the account rests on the cited branches rather than on a receipt.
Whether an application receives a distinguishable error before the fatal path is not established here; the guards are panics, and the API returns errors only for proposal-related rejections.
